U.S. adult obesity rose by nearly 12 percentage points between 2000 and 2018. The question is why.

By most measures, we aren’t eating more: Survey data find no significant increase in reported calorie intake in the last few decades.

Are we moving less? Among U.S. and European adults, energy spent on physical activity has actually increased.

He thinks changes in food quality, especially ultra-processing, may suppress thermogenesis, the energy we release as heat, through effects on the microbiome, brown fat, and muscle. That raises the possibility that what we eat affects how much energy we burn, not just how much we consume.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Fructose has a reputation as the sugar that goes straight to the liver, but it also reaches the gut first, and a short study in young, healthy adults showed how quickly that can matter. Three days of eating more fructose, with total calories held the same, was enough to raise bacterial endotoxin in their blood.

Blood from the gut drains straight to the liver, so what happens in the gut and what happens in the liver end up closely connected. In this study, researchers swapped some of the complex carbohydrate in a standardized diet for either fructose or glucose for three days at a time, kept calories steady, and gave everyone a washout period in between.

After the fructose days, endotoxin in the blood went up, and so did ALT, an enzyme that rises when liver cells are under strain, while markers of nitric oxide, which our blood vessels rely on to relax, went down. The immune cells in the blood also turned up the receptors that recognize endotoxin, leaving them primed and ready to react. None of this happened with the same amount of glucose, and nobody's weight changed with either sugar.

Endotoxin is a piece of the outer wall of certain gut bacteria, and normally very little of it gets past the intestinal lining. Fructose appears to loosen that lining and to favor the kinds of bacteria that make endotoxin, and once endotoxin reaches the blood, the liver is the first organ to meet it. Repeated exposure like this is one of the paths toward fatty liver and insulin resistance.

Three days is a shorter stretch than many people's usual week of sodas, juice and dessert, which is what makes the speed of this change worth noticing.

If someone is trying to protect their liver and their metabolic health, it's clear that the type of sugar matters, and cutting back on fructose-heavy foods and drinks helps protect the gut lining and the liver even when calories stay the same.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
James Engel started Ozempic in 2023 to manage his type 2 diabetes. Four months later he woke up with sudden vision loss in one eye. Doctors diagnosed non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION)—a rare “eye stroke” from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve that often causes permanent damage. 

He kept taking the drug, unaware of emerging signals linking GLP-1s to the condition. In October 2024 the other eye went. Now legally blind, Engel quit his job, lost his commercial driver’s license, and can no longer watch his grandkids play baseball or pursue the retirement travel he and his wife had planned. 

His case is not unique. Hundreds of people have filed lawsuits claiming Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound, and other GLP-1 drugs caused sudden NAION and vision loss, and that manufacturers failed to adequately warn patients and doctors. Those claims are consolidated in federal MDL 3163 in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania—roughly 278 cases pending as of early November 2026. Plaintiffs allege failure to warn, design defects, and related theories; the companies deny liability and note the absolute risk remains low. 

On November 9, 2026 the FDA required every GLP-1 product (semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, etc.) to add a warning about a potential increased risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section. 

In the agency’s analysis of 126 trials covering more than 134,000 patients, the rate was about 6.4 cases per 100,000 person-years on a GLP-1 versus 3.8 on placebo or other glucose-lowering drugs. Cases have been reported with every marketed GLP-1. The European Medicines Agency had already classified NAION as a very rare side effect of semaglutide (up to 1 in 10,000) and advised stopping the drug if it is confirmed. 
NAION is sudden, usually painless, and typically affects one eye. There is no proven treatment to reverse the vision loss. Risk factors overlap with those of many GLP-1 users (diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnea, older age, “disc at risk”). Absolute risk is small, but for the people who develop it the consequences are life-altering—as Engel’s story shows.
Patients are advised to report any sudden painless vision change, visual-field defects, or other disturbances immediately and seek urgent ophthalmology evaluation. Doctors are told to consider discontinuing the GLP-1 if NAION is diagnosed unless the benefits clearly outweigh the risk. 
The drugs remain widely used and effective for many. The new labeling and the growing lawsuits simply make one more rare but serious trade-off explicit.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Japan has one of the lowest obesity rates in the developed world. By the standard used almost everywhere else—BMI of 30 or higher—only about 4.6% of Japanese adults qualify. In the United States that number sits near 40%. Walk the streets of Tokyo or Osaka and the contrast is obvious: people are simply smaller.
Yet diabetes tells a different story. Age-adjusted prevalence sits around 8%, with more than 10 million adults affected. It is lower than the American rate, but strikingly high for a population that barely has obesity by international standards. The usual explanation—too much body fat—does not fully fit.
A large part of the answer lies in muscle. Skeletal muscle is the body’s primary glucose sink, responsible for roughly 70–80% of the glucose cleared under the influence of insulin. Less muscle means less storage capacity, even when total body weight looks favorable. East Asian populations, including the Japanese, tend to carry less skeletal muscle mass than Caucasian populations at the same BMI. They also store relatively more fat inside the abdomen and have, on average, a smaller reserve of insulin-producing beta cells. The result is that metabolic trouble can appear at BMIs in the low-to-mid 20s rather than the 30s.
Japanese studies repeatedly show the same pattern: people with low muscle mass plus a larger waist have several times the diabetes risk of those with more muscle and less abdominal fat. Diabetes itself then accelerates muscle loss, creating a cycle. High intakes of refined white rice and modest protein intakes over decades can further limit how much muscle is built and kept. Daily walking keeps overall weight down, but it does not always build the absolute muscle mass that functions as a large glucose buffer.
The Japanese example is useful precisely because it separates thinness from metabolic resilience. A low number on the scale is protective against the extremes seen in high-obesity countries, yet it is not enough on its own. Muscle is not optional equipment. It is the main organ that decides how much glucose stays in the blood after a meal. Where that organ is chronically undersized, diabetes risk remains higher than body weight alone would predict.

For decades, the story went like this: depression was a chemical imbalance, specifically low serotonin, and SSRIs fixed it by boosting that neurotransmitter. It was simple, marketable, and repeated so often it became medical common sense.

Then, in 2022, a team led by psychiatrist Joanna Moncrieff published a systematic umbrella review in Molecular Psychiatry. Instead of running one new experiment, they pulled together the major existing reviews and meta-analyses covering the main lines of serotonin research—levels in blood and spinal fluid, receptor binding, the serotonin transporter, genetic studies, and tryptophan-depletion experiments. 

The data involved tens of thousands of people.

What they found was striking for its absence. There was no consistent evidence that people with depression have lower serotonin activity or concentrations than people without it. Some of the largest, highest-quality genetic studies showed no link between the serotonin-transporter gene and depression, even when stress was factored in. 

Experiments that temporarily lowered serotonin availability did not reliably induce depression in healthy volunteers. In a few areas, the data even pointed the other way, or suggested that long-term antidepressant use itself might be associated with lower serotonin measures.

The authors’ conclusion was direct: the main areas of research provide no support for the hypothesis that depression is caused by lowered serotonin activity or concentrations. They did not claim antidepressants do nothing, nor that serotonin is irrelevant to mood. They simply showed that the classic “chemical imbalance” explanation—the one many patients had been told—was not backed by the accumulated evidence.

The paper landed like a quiet earthquake. For many, it was confirmation of long-held skepticism. For others, it raised uncomfortable questions about what exactly the most widely prescribed antidepressants are doing, and why the simple serotonin story had been so durable. The review didn’t end the debate, but it forced a clearer distinction between what the data actually show and the narrative that had dominated for decades.

The year is 2006.
A young researcher in Minnesota publishes a paper in Nature. He says he has found a special form of amyloid, the sticky protein that builds plaques in Alzheimer’s brains. He calls it Aβ*56. Inject it into young rats and their memory collapses. It looks like proof. The sticky stuff is not just sitting there. It is the cause.

The paper gets cited thousands of times. Money pours into amyloid drugs. The field lines up behind it.
Other labs try to find the same thing. They can’t. The protein is hard to see. The results refuse to repeat. Nobody says much. Careers are built on papers like this one.

In 2022 a doctor starts looking at the pictures. Western blots. Those dark bands that are supposed to prove a protein is there. Some of the bands are copies. Same noise, same edges, stuck into different places. Pieces cut from one experiment and pasted into another. An eraser tool used to clean up what did not fit. Experts call it shockingly blatant.

In 2024 the journal retracts the paper. Most of the authors agree the images were manipulated and the data cannot be trusted. The first author does not. In 2025 he leaves his job after more of his work is flagged for the same problem.

For nearly twenty years a set of doctored pictures helped steer research, funding, and drug trials. The amyloid idea was already old. This paper gave it fresh fuel and a clean story. The clean story was built from cut-and-paste.

The plaques were always real. The proof that one particular form of them caused the memory loss was not. Patients waited. The pictures did not.

Ancient Egyptian mummies show surprisingly high rates of atherosclerosis, according to the Horus studies that used CT scanning on dozens of remains spanning more than 2,000 years. In the initial work, 20 of 44 mummies with identifiable cardiovascular tissue had definite or probable atherosclerosis (about 45 percent). 

Later analyses found it in roughly 38 percent of 76 Egyptian mummies, and a 2024 global update reported it in 39 percent of 161. Calcifications appeared in the aorta, carotid, iliac, and even coronary arteries. One of the earliest documented cases of coronary atherosclerosis was a princess who lived around 1550–1580 BCE. Mean age at death was only about 40, yet rates rose sharply with age—most of those who reached the mid-40s or beyond showed arterial calcification.

This matters because the backbone of the ancient Egyptian diet was grain. Emmer wheat and barley were the primary crops. Bread and beer made from them were daily staples for virtually the entire population, from laborers to elites. Vegetables, legumes, and fruit supplemented the diet; meat (beef, wildfowl) was more available to the higher-status individuals who were typically mummified. Even so, the overall pattern was a grain-centered agricultural diet, not a modern ultra-processed one and not a hunter-gatherer one.

The findings undercut the idea that atherosclerosis is purely a disease of the modern West or that a grain- and plant-heavy pattern is inherently protective. Age was the strongest predictor, and similar rates of arterial calcification have turned up in other pre-industrial groups, including some hunter-gatherers, in the broader Horus work. That suggests an underlying human predisposition that diet and lifestyle can amplify. The Egyptian data simply show that a society built on bread and beer still produced plenty of calcified arteries thousands of years before processed food, tobacco, or sedentary office jobs existed.

Icelandic male centenarians lived long on fish, lamb, dairy, and butter — not salads. 
Iceland has some of the longest male life expectancy on the planet. The men who reached 100 did it on the diet the island actually produced for centuries: cold-water fish, lamb, beef, dairy, and butter. 

Fresh fruits and most vegetables were scarce. The climate and isolation made them unreliable or unavailable for most of the population’s history. 

One of the oldest documented Icelandic men (Georg, profiled in Men’s Health) got the vast majority of his calories from animal fat and protein — fish, lamb, beef, and dairy. Until middle age the only plants he regularly ate were potatoes, a few root vegetables, and rye bread. He also ate puffins, whale blubber, and heavily salted dried cod when available. 

He was not chasing “five a day.” 
Near-centenarian Stefan Thorliefsson (still swimming outdoors near 100) described a fish-heavy pattern, with occasional traditional items like boiled sheep’s head or fermented shark. The common thread is animal foods, not plant volume. 

Historical records confirm the pattern. For centuries the Icelandic diet was built on domestically produced animal foods (fish, dairy, butter, mutton) with little inclusion of vegetables. No local grains until later imports of rye. Pickling in whey, stockfish, smoked lamb, and skyr were staples. Fruits were limited to seasonal wild berries (crowberries, bilberries) when available; most people did not rely on them. 

Modern guidelines push 500–800 g of vegetables, fruits, and berries daily. That advice arrived long after the generations of Icelandic men who already reached advanced age on the opposite pattern. The island’s high life expectancy and male longevity track the traditional animal-based diet, not the later rise in imported produce. 
You do not need a plate full of plants to reach 100 when the animal foods are the foundation. The Icelandic record shows it.

Glucose does things other nutrients in the blood (i.e., amino acids and triglycerides) don't do. One of these is irreversibly binding proteins. Including binding to insulin! Glucose can bind to insulin itself, and the sugar-bound form of the hormone works less well than normal insulin.

When glucose lingers in the blood at high levels, it sticks to proteins in a process called glycation, which is the same process behind the A1c test, a measure of how much sugar has attached to hemoglobin in red blood cells. Well, insulin is a protein too.

People with type 2 diabetes have a glycated form of insulin circulating alongside the normal hormone, making up close to a tenth of the total. Infused into healthy men at the lower, everyday levels of insulin, it took substantially more of the glycated version to move the same amount of glucose out of the blood and into the tissues. 

This adds another way that high glucose and high insulin can reinforce each other. Higher blood glucose produces more glycated insulin, a weaker form of insulin pushes the pancreas to release even more of the hormone to keep glucose in check, and that chronically elevated insulin is itself a driver of insulin resistance.

If someone is hoping to keep their own insulin working as well as it should, it's clear that keeping blood glucose from staying high matters, and cutting back on the refined carbohydrates that drive it is the most direct way to do that.

On Saturated fat, Alzheimer's disease, and ApoE4 (600 words) 🧈👇

A common question I get is: Should ApoE4 carriers avoid saturated fat?

My yes/no answer is: No.

But let's unpack it.

First and foremost, the evidence is certainly not consistent across the literature. For example, a 2023 paper published in The Journal of Nutrition (PMID: 37778510) found that ApoE4 carriers consuming a higher-fat, lower-carbohydrate diet tended to have better cognitive performance.

Interestingly, among ApoE4 homozygotes, there was even a FAVORABLE association between a higher saturated-to-total-fat ratio and cognitive performance.

Now, I'm not suggesting that this is a consistent finding across the literature, or that this observational study establishes causality.

But that's precisely my point:

The notion that saturated fat is unequivocally harmful to cognitive health in ApoE4 carriers is not supported by a consistent, definitive body of evidence. (We will touch on heart health in a moment.)

🧠 The "Common Wisdom" is Not So Wise

So, where does the "common wisdom" that saturated fat is bad for ApoE4 carriers come from?

Well, largely from the fact that ApoE4 alters cholesterol metabolism and lipid trafficking, leading to the assumption that saturated fat will produce worse health outcomes in these individuals.

It’s a bit hand-wavy if you ask me. But that’s the explanation I’ve received when I’ve polled cardiologists.

Now, could we back this hypothesis with any data? 

Easy.

Because if you look at the general population eating mixed-macronutrient diets, higher saturated fat intake can cluster with other unhealthy dietary and lifestyle habits. So, of course, you're going to see associations between saturated fat intake and worse health outcomes in some populations.

But we should not make the all-too-common mistake of blaming the steak for what the milkshake and fries did. 

(Or pretending ‘statistical adjustments’ in nutritional epidemiology capture all the confounders. They’re just guestimates.)

❤️‍🔥 What about heart health?

But what about the lowest hanging fruit? Heart health?

Well, even if we shift our focus from the brain to the heart and assume a different chain of logic we still don't see a consistent signal that ApoE4 carriers respond differently to saturated fat.

For example, in one study comparing three diets controlled for cholesterol and unsaturated fat content, but varying in saturated fat intake (15%, 9%, and 6% of total calories), researchers found no evidence of a diet-by-genotype interaction across ApoE genotype strata (PMID: 9409276). 

The paper reads, “NO EVIDENCE of a significant diet by genotype interaction, however, could be identified for any of the measured lipid and lipoprotein end points” and “apoE genotype does not predict the magnitude of lipid response to reductions in dietary saturated fat.”

🧠 Could Saturated Fat Help?

Setting that aside, could we also explain the positive association between saturated fat and cognition seen in some studies?

Well, I think one plausible explanation is displacement.

If somebody is eating more of fatty foods, and as a result eating fewer carbohydrates, they might end up with better glycemic control and lower insulin levels over time.

And yes, insulin can cross the blood-brain barrier, and insulin-degrading enzyme (IDE) is involved in breaking down both insulin and amyloid-beta. So, there's a biologically plausible connection between insulin metabolism and amyloid clearance. 

But even setting that mechanism aside, insulin resistance is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to Alzheimer's disease pathology.

🧠 Practical Takeaways

At the end of the day, though, I think the most logical approach is to: 

👉Eat what most would call a whole-foods diet
👉Emphasize omega-3s (particularly for APOE4 carriers)
👉Cut sugar before worrying about saturated fat.

*For more nuances (and an actual plan) on how to protect your brain from Alzheimer's, see yesterday's letter. It's linked at the end of the attached thread 🧵👇

Humans didn't need bread to make it through the winter.

Farming and grain storage only go back about 11,000 years, and some of the oldest granaries ever found, near the Dead Sea, date right to that time.
